newsitem.title: USA: Pressure builds for U.S. campaign finance reform.
newsitem.headline: Pressure builds for U.S. campaign finance reform.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
With President Bill Clinton's Democratic Party mired in a campaign fundraising scandal, pressure is growing to reform a political finance system that almost all agree has virtually collapsed.

"The sickness of the campaign finance system has grown from something akin to a chronic fever to a medical emergency, a code blue situation," said Norman Ornstein, a political analyst with the American Enterprise Institute, a Washington think-tank.

The issue sprang to the centre of public attention in the final weeks of this year's presidential campaign with revelations that the Democratic Party raised large sums of money from foreign donors and individuals who could not substantiate the true source of the money they provided.

The party has been forced to return about $1.5 million and faces a Justice Department probe and the prospect of hearings in Congress next year. Clinton is also under the microscope amid allegations that overseas interests donated huge sums of money to influence the conduct of U.S. foreign policy.

"What we have now is the perception of corruption, a sense of government for sale," said Trevor Potter, former chairman of the Federal Election Commission, which is supposed to oversee the raising and spending of money on political campaigns but has become largely toothless and ineffective.

Past efforts to reform the system have foundered as Republicans and Democrats failed to agree on what could or should be done. In the past 10 years, lawmakers have amassed 6,742 pages of congressional testimony, 1,063 pages of committee reports and 113 votes -- all for naught.
But with Clinton and congressional leaders calling for reform, Potter said there was now some hope for progress.
The current system of campaign finance laws was put into place in the 1970s after the Watergate scandal that led to the resignation of President Richard Nixon.

Designed to prevent a small group of wealthy interests from dominating the political process, its guiding principle was to limit the amount of money one individual could contribute to any political candidate. That system, virtually everone agrees, is now in ruins.

Foreign money is just a small part of the problem. This year also saw an explosion of "soft money" flowing to both political parties. Unlike money that goes directly to political campaigns and is subject to legal limits, soft money comes from corporate coffers and labour unions and from wealthy individuals in unlimited amounts.

There used to be rules on how the political parties could spend this money. It was supposed to be devoted to strengthening grassroots political activity through voter registration and get-out-the-vote drives.

But Supreme Court decisions, including one this year, swept away those limitations. Political parties are now free to spend soft money on television advertisements or give it to interest groups for so-called issue advocacy campaigns.
In 1996, Democrats raised $102 million in soft money -- a jump of 232 percent over the last election cycle. Republicans increased their take by 166 percent to $121 million.

"This year we saw an explosion in the use of loopholes to get around election laws," Becky Cain, president of the League of Women Voters, said. "Millions of dollars of special interest money was used to influence the outcome of elections through the soft money, issue advocacy and independent expenditures loopholes."
Another relatively new phenomenon this year was the way interest groups decided to get involved in elections on their own, independent of political parties.

The AFL-CIO labour federation led the way, spending $35 million, much of it on negative television spots designed to defeat a targeted list of Republican members of Congress. A coalition of U.S. corporations responded in kind.

Meanwhile, environmentalists, pro and anti-abortion groups, anti-tax groups and others mounted their own television campaigns. Under U.S. law, as interpreted by the Supreme Court, all these groups were perfectly free to do this, as long as they did not specifically tell voters for whom they should vote.
